_meta.source: Derived: enso_regions, enso_model, crop_calendars, USDA PSD, World Bank Pink Sheet; live signals from JRC ASAP, GDACS, World Bank RTFP, ReliefWeb, El Niño news feed, trade_restrictions
_meta.notes: Tonnes first, on an ENSO-neutral baseline with USDA shown beside it; value at stake is tonnes × latest World Bank price, not a price forecast.
_meta.model_quality_rule: Computed from the past-winter test only (each pair refitted on earlier harvests, scored in tonnes against the no-El Niño yardstick). Supported: direction right with a coin-flip chance of 10% or less (6 of 7 winters), tonnes error below the yardstick's, and at most 1 false alarm (a predicted fall that became a rise). Moderate: direction right with a coin-flip chance of 25% or less (5 of 7) and tonnes error below the yardstick's. Exploratory: anything else, or not scored forward. Exploratory rows are kept but are not headline figures. The pairs were chosen on the full record, so even Supported is an upper bound on skill.

data.method: exp(fitted log-yield slope × ONI) − 1, applied to an ENSO-neutral production baseline, at two ONI values the record contains. Neutral baseline = the model's own trend yield for the harvest year (centred 9-year moving average of log yield, extended by its recent slope, no El Niño term) × harvested area (USDA's area for that harvest where USDA is the basis, else the latest FAOSTAT area), on USDA's basis where the marketing-year mapping is checked (enso_neutral.json). USDA's estimate is shown beside it, not multiplied: USDA may already allow for El Niño. The 90% range is coefficient uncertainty only; it does not include weather or forecast error. Value at stake = tonnes × latest World Bank price. No world-price model, no probability weighting.
data.neutral_source: Derived: FAOSTAT QCL (https://bulks-faostat.fao.org/production/Production_Crops_Livestock_E_All_Data_(Normalized).zip); USDA PSD bulk (https://apps.fas.usda.gov/psdonline/downloads/psd_grains_pulses_csv.zip and psd_oilseeds_csv.zip); fetched 2026-09-30; FAOSTAT licence CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO, USDA public domain
data.neutral_note: Change is applied to an ENSO-neutral trend baseline, not to USDA's estimate, so any allowance USDA already made for El Niño is not counted twice.
data.honesty: Estimates from a linear fit on December–February ONI. CPC's December–February 2026-27 median, RONI +2.36, is about ONI +2.3 to +3.0 given how the ONI–RONI gap moved in past El Niños. The strongest winter in the fit is ONI +2.5 (2015-16). A winter above it could bring larger changes than those shown.
data.q_nino_rule: A row is shown only when its El Niño slope passes Benjamini–Hochberg control on its own: q < 0.10 across all 146 fitted pairs.

regions.label: Southern Africa · maize
regions.precedent: Niño3.4 explains 45–53% of seasonal rainfall variance (Funk et al. 2016). r≈−0.53/−0.56 for rainfall. 2015-16: regional maize ~7.2 Mt, 27% below the prior year and 38% below the 5-year average. 2023-24: Zimbabwe maize −72%, Zambia −54%, South Africa yield −17%. 2026 outlook: SADC’s SARCOF-33 statement from 28 Aug 2026 favours below-normal October–December rainfall across most of the region, but normal to above-normal rainfall in northern Zambia, central Malawi and northern Mozambique, with above-normal rainfall in the extreme north of Zambia and Malawi; the broad dry signal continues into January–March 2027.

regions.label: India · kharif rice and the summer monsoon
regions.precedent: Monsoon rainfall–Niño3.4 correlation r≈−0.6; drought severity −2.0σ in El Niño years vs −1.3σ otherwise. Base rate of a deficient monsoon in an El Niño year is reported anywhere between 45% and 70% and is genuinely disputed. 2026 outlook: IMD’s 17 Sep 2026 extended-range bulletin reports all-India rainfall 15% below the long-period average from 1 Jun to 16 Sep 2026 and expects El Niño to strengthen through the remaining monsoon season; this is a season-to-date assessment, not a final monsoon total or a crop-loss estimate.

regions.label: Peru · anchoveta fishery
regions.precedent: The least contested ENSO-economic link in this compiled set, the 1972 anchoveta collapse is documented in the fisheries and the economics literature alike. Anchoveta catch fell from 10.3 Mt (1971) to 4.4 Mt (1972); biomass fell from 5.8 Mt to 1.2 Mt in 1997-98; Peru cancelled the entire first 2023-24 season, with a tac of 1.09 Mt against a 4.4 Mt/yr non-event average, >$1.4 bn in lost export sales and about 0.5% of Peruvian GDP. Peru's 2023 coastal El Niño cut GDP growth by 1.1 pp.
